scope: Six available contrast groups, two listening rounds per group; same selection for free and paid access. This is a starting-point sample, not a whole-language proficiency test.

selectionPolicy.basis: L1 inventory-transfer prediction with direct population/feature study support where listed
selectionPolicy.weightMeaning: Editorial priority weights, not probabilities, calibrated error rates or empirical rankings. Four-point study bonus selects studied contrasts but does not claim those are hardest.
selectionPolicy.diversity: At most two groups per feature family, except up to three tone groups. Sparse available banks may relax this only to fill the sample.
selectionPolicy.fallback: Same target/native language, unknown or Other native language uses broad editorial defaults. Missing production groups are skipped.
selectionPolicy.scoring: Answers and scores are never altered to cause failure or motivate purchase.

evidenceLevels.direct-study-supported: Primary research directly tested the relevant population and contrast. The current word list, short diagnostic and ordering are not validated by that fact.
evidenceLevels.predicted: Editorial cross-inventory inference. No direct L1-L2 empirical difficulty ranking is asserted.
evidenceLevels.broad-sample: Target-language sample with no L1 difficulty claim.
evidenceLevels.study-feature-supported: Primary research tested the relevant population and sound categories or feature in a broader identification task; this is not evidence that the exact binary contrast was separately tested.

sources.title: Logan, Lively & Pisoni (1991): Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/: A first report
sources.whatItSupports: Japanese adults; natural /r–l/ words, varied speakers and phonetic environments; held-out words and speaker tests.
sources.limitations: Identification training with visible alternatives, not this product’s cross-word audio-only ABX. Small initial study. Full stimulus table not recovered in this pass.

sources.title: Lambacher et al. (2001): Identification of English voiceless fricatives by Japanese listeners: The influence of vowel context on sensitivity and response bias
sources.whatItSupports: 104 Japanese listeners identified /f,s,ʃ,θ,h/ in varied syllable/vowel contexts. Confusions motivate /θ–s/, /ʃ–s/ and /f–h/.
sources.limitations: Perception study, not an intervention trial. Stimuli were nonsense syllables; our real words are editorial. Vowel context materially changes difficulty, especially /ʃ–s/ near /i/ and /f–h/ near /u/.

sources.title: Nishi & Kewley-Port (2008): Non-native speech perception training using vowel subsets: Effects of vowels in sets and order of training
sources.whatItSupports: Fifteen Korean listeners received nine-category American English vowel identification training. The vowel inventory includes /i,ɪ,ɛ,æ/. Japanese results are discussed from the earlier 2007 study.
sources.limitations: Korean population/feature evidence, not a dedicated binary /i-ɪ/ or /æ-ɛ/ diagnostic validation. No Japanese direct bonus is drawn from this 2008 source.

sources.title: Levy (2009), On the assimilation-discrimination relationship in American English adults’ French vowel learning
sources.whatItSupports: Three American English groups differing in French experience discriminated French vowel pairs; Figure 2 explicitly includes /y-u/, /y-i/, and /œ-ɛ/, alongside eight other pairs.
sources.limitations: Contexts were bilabial /rabVp/ and alveolar /radVt/. Tested pair membership is verified, but difficulty varies by context and experience; this does not validate our words, recordings or ordering.

sources.title: Kingston (2003), Learning Foreign Vowels
sources.whatItSupports: American-English learners, 12 German nonlow vowel categories, identification training with five speakers and varied consonantal frames.
sources.limitations: Words and pseudowords in stressed CVCn frames. No full lexical bank recovered. Inventory coverage does not prove every selected binary contrast below was separately trained.

sources.title: Gao et al. (2019), Perception of German tense and lax vowel contrast by Chinese learners
sources.whatItSupports: Seven tense/lax vowel pairs; Mandarin-Chinese listeners and German controls; quality/duration manipulations.
sources.limitations: Perception experiment with synthesized words, not HVPT. Full 70-word list not recovered; no word below is claimed as its stimulus.

sources.title: Herd, Jongman & Sereno: Perceptual and production training of intervocalic /d, ɾ, r/ in American English learners of Spanish
sources.whatItSupports: Direct L2 training of three intervocalic contrasts; generalization measures.
sources.limitations: Identification used written choices. Does not validate text-free cross-word ABX. Published article does not provide the full lexical table; candidate words are not labeled table-confirmed stimuli.

sources.title: De Iacovo et al.: The perception of gemination in Italian by first-language speakers in Italy and heritage and second-language speakers in Australia
sources.whatItSupports: L2 singleton/geminate perception; explicitly names papa/pappa, fata/fatta, paca/pacca.
sources.limitations: Synthetic and duration-manipulated identification experiment; not a training intervention. Named words occur in methods prose, not a lexical table; stimulusSourceIds deliberately empty under table-only policy.

sources.title: Smirnova Henriques et al.: The perception of Brazilian Portuguese open and close mid vowels by native Russian speakers
sources.whatItSupports: Table-confirmed real words for stressed e/ɛ and o/ɔ; Russian-L1 perception difficulty.
sources.limitations: Perception assessment, not training efficacy. Loanword and nonminimal contexts were not imported. Full IPA below is editorial normalization; tables mark target vowels.

sources.title: Martinez, Goad & Dow: L1 phonological effects on L2 (non-)naïve perception: a cross-language investigation of the oral–nasal vowel contrast in Brazilian Portuguese
sources.whatItSupports: L1-dependent oral–nasal perception across French, English and Spanish varieties.
sources.limitations: Artificial monosyllables: not evidence for real-word pools or the proposed low-vowel pair.

sources.title: Vita Kogan: The Effect of First Language Perception on the Discrimination of a Non-native Vowel Contrast: Investigating Individual Differences
sources.whatItSupports: Russian i/ɨ perception examined in 68 Spanish participants against a Russian baseline; vowel tokens were spliced and rated for dissimilarity.
sources.limitations: Non-native perception assessment, not a training efficacy experiment. Most Spanish participants reported some basic foreign-language knowledge. No word pool below is attributed as its stimulus list.

sources.title: Tajima et al. (2008): Training English listeners to perceive phonemic length contrasts in Japanese
sources.whatItSupports: Vowel-length identification training and tests of rate, word position, presentation context and transfer. Results support treating those variables explicitly.
sources.limitations: Reported generalization was limited. Identification with feedback is not our cross-word audio-only ABX; the paper does not establish its superiority. No word-list membership imported here.

sources.title: Tsukada, Hirata & Roengpitya (2014): Cross-language perception of Japanese vowel length contrasts
sources.whatItSupports: American English, Italian and Thai listeners were tested on Japanese vowel length with AXB discrimination.
sources.limitations: Abstract inspected; full stimulus list not recovered. Evidence concerns the length class, not every vowel-specific bank or training success. No word receives stimulus provenance from it.

sources.title: Fougeron & Smith (1993), French: Illustrations of the IPA
sources.whatItSupports: Parisian vowel/consonant inventory, mid-vowel distributions, nasal notation and rhotic variation.
sources.limitations: Descriptive reference, not learner outcome evidence or certification of this word bank.

sources.title: Avelino: Mexico City Spanish
sources.whatItSupports: Mexican Spanish inventory and contextual variation.
sources.limitations: Descriptive phonology; neither a training trial nor verification of every proposed lemma.

sources.title: Bertinetto & Loporcaro: The sound pattern of Standard Italian, as compared with Florence, Milan and Rome
sources.whatItSupports: Standard Italian length and stressed mid-vowel contrasts.
sources.limitations: Regional lexical distributions differ. Predictable vowel duration is not an independent vowel-length contrast.

sources.title: Barbosa & Albano: Brazilian Portuguese
sources.whatItSupports: Reference target variety for existing Brazilian Portuguese pools.
sources.limitations: Full text not extracted here; new rhotic candidates require a chosen regional realization.

sources.title: Lee & Zee: Standard Chinese (Beijing)
sources.whatItSupports: Reference for target-variety inventory.
sources.limitations: Publisher HTML record accessed; full phonetic illustration not extracted. New consonant pools remain editorial candidates pending complete source and lexical checks.

sources.title: Okada (1991): Japanese — Illustrations of the IPA
sources.whatItSupports: Tokyo-area sound inventory, length contrasts, predictable consonant variants, high-vowel devoicing and independent pitch accent.
sources.limitations: Descriptive illustration of one speaker, not learner-training evidence. Our IPA conventions normalize its older symbols and omit pitch labels. No recordings reused.

sources.title: Moscow State University phonetics: meaning-distinguishing role of consonant hardness/softness
sources.whatItSupports: Explicit hard-onset [mɨl] versus soft-onset [mʲil] coupling.
sources.limitations: Pedagogical phonetic description, not a training trial. Its articulatory classification should not be treated as the only theoretical analysis.

sources.title: Möbius & Trouvain (2014), Phonology, Saarland University
sources.whatItSupports: German minimal-pair examples, inventories, contextual ich/ach allophones and final neutralization.
sources.limitations: University phonetics teaching material, not an L2 outcome experiment.

sources.title: University of Saarland eLAUT: American English (California) sound inventory
sources.whatItSupports: Reference inventory and selected example words for American consonant/vowel contrasts.
sources.limitations: University phonetics teaching resource, not L2 efficacy evidence. California inventory does not license every British distinction; contrast-level dialect restrictions override it.

sources.title: Schwab and Dellwo (2017): Intonation and talker variability in the discrimination of Spanish lexical stress contrasts by Spanish, German and French listeners
sources.whatItSupports: Native French (N=27), German (N=21), Spanish (N=17) listeners completed 216 odd-one-out trials of Spanish disyllabic words contrasting lexical stress. French listeners performed above chance without intonation variability and at chance with it.
sources.limitations: Task and intonation conditions differ from this product. Supports French-background stress sampling, not a fixed expected error rate or a universal impairment.

sources.title: Effects of First Language Background and Learning Experience in Perceiving Mandarin Lexical Tones (2022)
sources.whatItSupports: English and Japanese backgrounds compared on all six Mandarin tone pairs.
sources.limitations: Relative performance depends on pair and learning experience. Chosen tone subset/order is editorial, not a published six-item diagnostic.

sources.title: Thelwall and Sa’Adeddin (1990), Arabic, Illustrations of the IPA
sources.whatItSupports: Standard Arabic consonant/vowel inventory, quantity contrasts and absence of native /p/ and /v/.
sources.limitations: Broad prediction only; regional Arabic, loanwords and learner experience differ. Not L2 perceptual ranking.

sources.title: Ohala (1994), Hindi, Illustrations of the IPA
sources.whatItSupports: Standard Hindi inventory and contrasts, including quantity, nasal vowels and laryngeal distinctions.
sources.limitations: /v-w/ and other L2 priority weights are predictions; regional Hindi and bilingual experience differ.

sources.title: Cho, Jun and Ladefoged (2002), Acoustic and aerodynamic correlates of Korean stops and fricatives
sources.whatItSupports: Korean laryngeal contrast differs from a simple English voiced/voiceless opposition.
sources.limitations: Does not empirically rank all Korean-to-L2 contrasts; Seoul and regional/age differences matter.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: The Korean Alphabet, Hangeul
sources.whatItSupports: Korean consonant and vowel categories for inventory-based predictions.
sources.limitations: Not an L2 perception study. /r-l/, labiodental and vowel priorities are editorial predictions, not measured rates.

limitations: Not all 108 native-to-target combinations have direct study evidence. All nonlisted selections are predictions.
Prior L2 experience, dialect, individual perception and task can override L1-based expectations.
Broad labels are coarse: Spanish dental fricatives vary geographically, Arabic covers many varieties, Korean vowel length varies by age/region, and Portuguese covers different vowel systems.
German curriculum currently offers almost entirely vowel contrasts; apparent vowel concentration reflects available bank coverage.
Mandarin bank contains tones and segmental contrasts but this short sample does not assess tone sandhi or connected speech.
Two observations per group have high uncertainty; do not describe a low result as a diagnosed deficit or proficiency level.

Nishi 2008 is used only as Korean population/feature evidence; the Japanese vowel direct bonuses were removed. French /y-i/ and /œ-ɛ/ tested membership was independently verified in Levy 2009 Figure 2. Study-feature support is separate from exact-contrast support.

finalEvidenceAudit.japaneseVowelOverrides: Removed; retained as inventory predictions, not cited to Korean 2008 sample.
finalEvidenceAudit.frenchVowels: Verified /y-u/, /y-i/, /œ-ɛ/ explicitly present in primary Levy 2009 Figure 2 discrimination pairs.
finalEvidenceAudit.frenchSpanishStress: Verified French N=27, German N=21, Spanish N=17 and Spanish disyllabic lexical-stress odd-one-out task in Schwab and Dellwo 2017 abstract.
finalEvidenceAudit.inventorySources: No inventory-only source confers a direct-study bonus.
